title: Covered calls and protective puts
objectives: Combine options with the stock and match each to a view.
See a covered call as a short put and a protective put as a long call.

screens.prose: You own a share you bought at £100.00. You sell a call on it, struck at £110.00, and collect £3.00. The steep dashed line is the share alone; the other is the call you sold. The bold line is your total profit.
screens.question: The share ends at £120.00. What is your total profit?

widget.label: Total profit
widget.accept: £13.00: +£20.00 on the share, +£3.00 premium, −£10.00 on the call

hints.text: Add the share's gain, the premium and what you owe on the call.
The call's buyer exercises: you sell for £110.00 a share worth £120.00.
Share +20, premium +3, call −10.

feedback.correct: +£20.00 on the share, +£3.00 premium, −£10.00 on the call.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the share, the premium and the exercised call.

byKey.nocall: You kept the share's whole rise and the premium. The call's buyer takes your share at £110.00.
byKey.shareonly: That is the share alone. You also collected £3.00 and owe £10.00 on the call.
byKey.nopremium: You forgot the £3.00 you collected when you sold the call.

explain.text: The share gains £20.00 and the premium adds £3.00. The call costs you £10.00, because you must sell at £110.00. The total is £13.00.

screens.prose: Slide the price at expiry across the range and watch the bold line. Compare it with the share alone.
screens.question: What happens to your profit above £110.00?

options.text: It stays at £13.00, however high the share goes
It keeps rising with the share
options.why: That is the share alone. Above £110.00 the sold call takes every extra pound.

options.text: It falls, because the sold call loses you money
options.why: The call costs £1.00 more for each pound, but the share gains £1.00 too. They cancel.

hints.text: Compare the label at £115.00 and at £125.00.
Look to the right of the call's strike.

feedback.correct: Above £110.00 the share's gains go to the call's buyer.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide above £110.00 and compare two prices.

explain.text: Above £110.00 every pound the share gains, the call takes away. Below it you hold the share with £3.00 of cushion. Your gain is capped at $110 - 100 + 3 = 13$.

screens.prose: A share held with a call sold against it is a **covered call**: the share covers what you might owe. Investors write them for the premium. The break-even marker is hidden.
screens.question: At what price at expiry does the covered call break even?

widget.label: Break-even price
widget.accept: £97.00: the £100.00 purchase price less the £3.00 premium

hints.text: Below £110.00 your profit is the share's gain plus £3.00.

feedback.correct: The £3.00 premium cushions the first £3.00 of a fall.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the share's loss uses up the premium.

byKey.entry: You ignored the £3.00 premium. It cushions the first £3.00 of a fall.
byKey.added: You added the premium to the price. You received it, so it lowers the break-even.
byKey.strike: That is where the cap starts. You are already £13.00 up there.

explain.text: The premium cushions the first £3.00 of a fall. So you break even at $100 - 3 = 97$. The covered call is income now, paid for by a cap later.

screens.prose: Fill in the table. The share column is your profit on the share. The call column is your profit on the sold call, premium included.
screens.question: Complete the profit table for the covered call.

hints.text: Below £110.00 the sold call is just the £3.00 you kept.
At £130.00 you owe $130 - 110 = 20$ on the call.

feedback.correct: A flat £13.00 above the strike, and nearly the share's full loss below.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Do the share and the call separately, then add.

byKey.r0c2: At £80.00 the call is not exercised. You keep the £3.00 premium.
byKey.r0c3: Add across: −20 on the share and +3 on the call.
byKey.r3c2: You collected £3.00 but owe £20.00 when the call is exercised at £130.00.
byKey.r3c3: Add across: +30 on the share and −17 on the call.

explain.text: Below £110.00 the call is a flat £3.00 of income. Above it, the call gives back the share's extra gains. In a fall the covered call loses almost as much as the share: −£17.00 at £80.00.

screens.prose: Insurance instead. You own the share bought at £100.00 and buy a put struck at £95.00 for £2.00. A colleague says the put removes all loss. The share crashes to £70.00.
screens.question: What is your total profit at £70.00?

options.why: You treated the put as removing all loss. It floors the share at £95.00, not £100.00, and it cost £2.00.
You counted the gap to the strike but not the £2.00 premium.
You counted the premium but not the £5.00 gap between £100.00 and £95.00.
That is the share alone. The put lets you sell it for £95.00.

hints.text: The put lets you sell at £95.00. What do you lose on the share then?
You also paid £2.00 for the put.
−5 on the share, sold at £95.00, and −2 for the put.

feedback.correct: −£5.00 to the strike and −£2.00 for the put.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the gap down to the strike and the cost of the put.

byKey.b: The put does not refund the fall from £100.00 to £95.00, or its own price.
byKey.c: The put was not free. Take off its £2.00 too.

explain.text: The put sells your share at £95.00, so the share loses only £5.00. Add the £2.00 premium: the floor is −£7.00, however far the share falls. A **protective put** limits the loss; it does not remove it.

screens.prose: Here is the protective put's profit line again: share bought at £100.00, £95.00 put bought for £2.00. Look at its shape, not its legs.
screens.question: Which single option has the same profit diagram?

options.text: A long call struck at £95.00, costing £7.00
A long put struck at £95.00, costing £2.00
options.why: A long put gains as the share falls. This line gains as the share rises.
A short put has a capped gain and a large loss below. This line has a floor below and no cap.

options.text: A long call struck at £100.00, costing £2.00
options.why: The kink is at £95.00, the put's strike. The floor is −£7.00, so the call must cost £7.00.

hints.text: Where is the kink, and how low is the floor?
Flat to the left, slope 1 to the right: that is a call's shape.
Kink at £95.00, floor at −£7.00: a £95.00 call bought for £7.00.

feedback.correct: A floor, a kink at £95.00 and slope 1 above: a £95.00 call at £7.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the kink and the floor, then think which option has that shape.

explain.text: Below £95.00 the profit is flat at −£7.00; above, it rises £1.00 a pound. That is a call struck at £95.00 costing £7.00. Share plus put looks like a call: **put-call parity** in pictures, derived in level 3.

screens.prose: Combine both. Hold the share bought at £100.00, buy the £95.00 put for £2.00 and sell the £110.00 call for £3.00. This is a **collar**: the call pays for the put.
screens.question: Fill in the collar's key numbers.

hints.text: Net the premiums first: one received, one paid.
Below £95.00 the put sells your share at £95.00; above £110.00 the call takes it at £110.00.

feedback.correct: +£1.00 net, a floor at −£4.00 and a cap at +£11.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Net the premiums, then check the share at each strike.

byKey.r0c1: You receive £3.00 for the call and pay £2.00 for the put.
byKey.r1c1: Below £95.00 you sell at £95.00: −5 on the share, plus the £1.00 net premium.
byKey.r2c1: Above £110.00 you sell at £110.00: +10 on the share, plus the £1.00 net premium.

explain.text: The sold call pays for the put with £1.00 to spare. Every outcome lands between −£4.00 and +£11.00. A cheap floor, paid for by giving up the upside.

screens.prose: The table shows each position's profit at three expiry prices. Each was built on a share bought at £100.00.
screens.question: Match each position to the view it suits.

slots.label: Extra income if the share stays flat
Insurance against a fall, keeping the upside
A cheap floor, giving up gains above a cap

hints.text: Read the £100.00 column for a flat market.
Compare the £80.00 column for protection and the £125.00 column for upside.
Covered call earns most when flat; protective put keeps £23.00 of upside; the collar is cheap but capped.

feedback.correct: Income, insurance and a cheap floor.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use one column per view.

byKey.t1: The covered call makes the most at £100.00, from its premium.
byKey.t2: The protective put loses least of the two that keep the upside, and still makes £23.00 at £125.00.
byKey.t3: The collar has the highest floor, −£4.00, but stops at £11.00.
byKey.t4: The share alone has no protection and no income, so it fits none of these views.

explain.text: Flat at £100.00, the covered call's premium makes it the best. In a fall the protective put and the collar both floor the loss, but only the put keeps the rise. The collar's floor is cheapest because its cap paid for it.

screens.prose: You priced each position leg by leg. As payoffs at expiry: $$S_T - \max(S_T - K, 0) = K - \max(K - S_T, 0),$$ $$S_T + \max(K - S_T, 0) = K + \max(S_T - K, 0).$$ A covered call has a short put's shape, and a protective put a long call's.
screens.question: The covered call (share at £100.00, £110.00 call sold for £3.00) has the same profit diagram as which position?

options.text: A short put struck at £110.00, sold for £13.00

options.why: A short call loses as the share rises. The covered call gains up to £13.00.
A long put gains as the share falls. The covered call loses then.

options.text: A short put struck at £100.00, sold for £3.00
options.why: The kink is at the call's strike, £110.00, and the best case is £13.00.

feedback.correct: Below £110.00 both give $S_T - 97$; above, both give £13.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the kink and the cap.

explain.text: Below £110.00 the covered call makes $S_T - 97$, and above it a flat £13.00. A £110.00 put sold for £13.00 gives exactly that. Equal payoffs mean equal prices, the core of put-call parity.

screens.prose: A pension fund holds £10m of a share at £50.00: 200,000 shares. It writes calls struck 10% above the market, at £55.00, for 2% premium income: £1.00 a share. Three months later the share is at £60.00.
screens.question: What is the fund's total profit on the shares and the calls?

hints.text: Work per share first, then multiply by 200,000.
Per share: the share gains £10.00, the premium adds £1.00, and the call costs $60 - 55 = 5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Per share, add the share's gain and the premium, and take off the call's payoff.

byKey.free: You treated the premium as free income on top of the full rise. Above £55.00 the calls take the extra £5.00 a share.
byKey.shareonly: That is the shares alone, without the calls the fund wrote.
byKey.nopremium: You forgot the £1.00 a share the fund collected.

explain.text: Per share: +£10.00 on the share, +£1.00 premium, −£5.00 on the calls, so £6.00. On 200,000 shares that is £1,200,000, against £2,000,000 unhedged. The £200,000 of income cost £1,000,000 of upside.

screens.prose: Before a known event, a risk desk hedges a holding with 3-month puts. It checks every hedge with a payoff table. A leg is `(kind, qty, strike)`: `kind` is `"call"`, `"put"` or `"stock"`, and `qty` is negative when short. A stock leg pays `qty * S` and ignores its strike.
screens.question: Complete `payoff(legs, S)` so it returns the total payoff at expiry. `table` then works as written.

widget.how: Submit runs 10 hidden tests: spreads, straddles, butterflies and share-plus-option positions, short legs and an empty list. Each value is accepted when math.isclose holds.

hints.text: A call pays `max(S - strike, 0)` and a put `max(strike - S, 0)`.
Multiply each leg's payoff by its `qty`, so short legs count against you.

feedback.correct: One loop covers every position, long or short.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each kind's payoff and the sign of `qty`.

explain.text: A short leg is a negative quantity, so one formula covers both sides. With the stock leg, the protective put pays $\max(S_T, 95)$: a floor at the strike. `table` just maps that over the prices.

ideas: A covered call adds premium income now but caps the gain above the strike.
A protective put floors the loss at the gap to the strike plus the premium. It does not remove it.
Share plus short call looks like a short put, and share plus long put like a long call: put-call parity in pictures.

formula.name: Protective put payoff
formula.note: A floor at $K$; profit floor $K - S_0 - P$.

summary.trap: A covered call is not free income: it sells your upside. A protective put still loses the premium and the gap to the strike.

quiz.prose: A share trades at £100.00. Someone offers you a put struck at £100.00, expiring in a month, for £0.00.
quiz.question: Why can no such offer last?

options.text: Its payoff is never negative and sometimes positive, so everyone would take it
A put struck at today's price is always worthless
options.why: At expiry the share may be below £100.00, and then the put pays.

options.text: It is fine: the seller collects nothing but takes no risk
options.why: The seller owes $100 - S_T$ whenever the share falls. Nobody takes that risk for nothing.

options.text: Only calls can be struck at today's price
options.why: Puts and calls can both be struck at the money.

feedback.correct: A free floor would be a free chance of gain with no risk.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does the put pay at worst and at best?

explain.text: The put pays $\max(100 - S_T, 0)$, never below 0 and positive after any fall. Something that can only help you cannot cost nothing. A free floor would be an arbitrage.

quiz.prose: You hold a share bought at £100.00 and sell the £105.00 call on it for £2.00.
quiz.question: What is the most you can make at expiry?

widget.label: Maximum profit
widget.accept: £7.00: £5.00 up to the strike plus the £2.00 premium

feedback.correct: £5.00 to the strike plus the £2.00 premium.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the share's gain up to the strike and the premium.

byKey.premium: That is the premium alone. The share can also gain £5.00 before the cap.
byKey.nocap: Above £105.00 the call's buyer takes the share. Your gain stops there.

explain.text: Above £105.00 your share is called away at £105.00, a £5.00 gain. With the £2.00 premium the cap is £7.00.

quiz.prose: You hold a share bought at £50.00 and buy the £45.00 put for £1.50.
quiz.question: What is your worst profit at expiry?

widget.label: Worst profit
widget.accept: −£6.50: −£5.00 to the strike and −£1.50 for the put

feedback.correct: The gap to the strike plus the premium.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the fall to the strike and the cost of the put.

byKey.premium: You counted the premium but not the £5.00 fall down to the strike.
byKey.none: The put does not remove all loss. It floors the share at £45.00.

explain.text: Below £45.00 the put sells your share at £45.00, a £5.00 loss. With the £1.50 premium the floor is −£6.50.

quiz.prose: A fund holds 10,000 shares at £20.00 and fears a court ruling next month. It buys 3-month puts struck at £19.00, at £0.40 a share.
quiz.question: What is the most the fund can lose on the hedged holding by the puts' expiry?

feedback.correct: £1.00 to the strike plus £0.40, on 10,000 shares.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work per share, then multiply.

byKey.premium: That is the cost of the puts alone. The share can also fall £1.00 to the strike.
byKey.gap: That is the fall to the strike. The puts cost £4,000 as well.
byKey.none: The puts floor the loss; they do not remove it.

explain.text: Per share the worst case is $(20 - 19) + 0.40 = 1.40$. On 10,000 shares that is £14,000, whatever the ruling.
